units.text: You hear a noise in an empty house. The mind immediately seeks something that produced it. In many situations this reflex is useful. But ‘what produced it?’ can turn too quickly into ‘who wanted to produce it?’ Between detecting a relationship and attributing an intention lies a difference that language easily hides.

Psychology offers no single verdict on why people believe in laws of nature. Research studies more bounded processes: pattern identification, explanations of properties, responses to uncertainty and how people generalize. Applying these to the metaphysics of laws is an interpretation that must be announced, not a direct experimental result.

Cimpian and Salomon propose the ‘inherence heuristic’: a tendency to explain some patterns through supposedly inherent characteristics of things without sufficiently examining history and external conditions. It is a theoretical framework supported by several research lines, not a universal law of judgment. A social pattern may seem natural because we attribute its cause to a group’s nature, although the conventions producing it should also be investigated (Cimpian și Salomon, 2014) .

The connection to our topic is clear, but it is an extrapolation: ‘that is how things are’ can stop exploration of mechanisms. If a child asks why a social role is more often occupied by a particular group, ‘because those people are made for it’ sounds explanatory. In reality, it may close precisely the investigation of access, selection, learning and expectations.

Whitson and Galinsky reported, across six experiments, a connection between lack of control and illusory pattern perception in different tasks. The result became attractive for the idea that the mind compensates for uncertainty with order. But this story must not be presented as definitive fact (Whitson și Galinsky, 2008) .

Van Elk and Lodder reported seven conceptual-replication experiments in which they did not find expected effects on the measures used. Their analyses questioned the robustness of control manipulations and indicated publication-bias problems in the examined literature. This does not prove that the need for control never matters. It shows that an elegant psychological explanation can be more fragile than its popularity (Van Elk și Lodder, 2018) .

It is a perfect lesson for a book about laws: we cannot combat naive belief in regularities by ourselves using an insufficiently verified psychological regularity. The psychology of science must undergo the same discipline it demands of science.

There is also a deeper logical error. Suppose someone believes in a law because they need security. This psychological origin does not imply the law is false. A person may believe something true for a weak reason and something false for an intelligent reason. A belief’s genealogy and testing its content are different investigations.

How might the effect of the word ‘law’ be studied more directly? Here is a proposal, not an experiment already conducted: participants receive the same numerical regularity labeled either ‘law’, ‘provisional model’ or ‘observed pattern’. They are then asked how far they generalize, which counterexamples they accept and which interventions they consider possible. Wording, numerical competence and source prestige should be controlled, and hypotheses and analysis established before seeing results.

An interesting result would be if the label ‘law’ changed confidence even when data and precision were identical. Absence of an effect would be equally important. It should be repeated across languages, contexts and populations before we speak of a general mechanism. A student study cannot directly establish the psychology of all societies.

Education could train two complementary reflexes: courage to seek regularities and patience to put them to the test. Telling students ‘think critically’ is not enough. We must give them cases where a seductive explanation and a correct one make different predictions, then let them observe the difference.

The mind needs compression: we cannot preserve every experience as an episode unrelated to the rest. The danger is not the existence of mental patterns. It is forgetting the distinction between a reassuring pattern and one that survived a serious attempt to contradict it.
